title: Image Segmentation — Thresholding & Contours
aim: Compare Global, Otsu's automatic, and Adaptive thresholding, and annotate detected objects with bounding boxes.
coreConcept: Segmentation partitions an image into foreground and background. **Global thresholding** uses one cutoff for the whole image; **Otsu's method** computes it automatically from the histogram; **Adaptive thresholding** uses a different cutoff for each neighbourhood to handle uneven lighting.
formula:
Global: g(x, y) = 255 \text{ if } f(x, y) > T, \text{ else } 0
Otsu: T^* = \arg\max_T \left[ w_0(T) \, w_1(T) \, (\mu_0 - \mu_1)^2 \right]
Adaptive: T(x, y) = \text{mean}(N_{xy}) - C
intuition: Think of segmenting as a pair of scissors. **Global** works when lighting is even — one cut separates every object. **Otsu** picks the sharpest cut in the histogram automatically. **Adaptive** slides the scissors locally, so a shadow doesn't ruin the whole cut.
procedure: Load an image with clearly separated objects (coins, cells, printed text).
Apply **Global threshold** at T = 127 and see what survives.
Slide the global threshold and find a value where objects separate cleanly.
Apply **Otsu** — it picks T automatically. Compare with your manual pick.
Apply **Adaptive threshold** — observe that uneven lighting no longer matters.
Toggle **Bounding boxes** to annotate each detected object.
Compare all three methods side by side.
theory:
Thresholding converts a grayscale image to binary. It assumes the histogram is **bimodal** — one peak for background, one for foreground.

- **Global threshold** — a single cutoff $T$. Fast but fails when lighting is uneven.
- **Otsu's method** — searches for $T$ that maximises **between-class variance**. Works when the histogram is clearly bimodal.
- **Adaptive threshold** — computes $T(x, y)$ per pixel as the local mean minus a constant $C$. Immune to smooth lighting gradients.

After thresholding, **connected components** (or contour detection) group foreground pixels into objects. Bounding boxes annotate each component.

### When to use what

| Lighting | Best method |
|---|---|
| Uniform | Global or Otsu |
| Uneven (shadows, gradient) | Adaptive |
| Bimodal histogram | Otsu |
| OCR / scanned text | Adaptive |
pythonCode:
import cv2
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

img = cv2.imread('coins.png', cv2.IMREAD_GRAYSCALE)
blur = cv2.GaussianBlur(img, (5, 5), 0)

# Global
_, th_global = cv2.threshold(blur, 127, 255, cv2.THRESH_BINARY)

# Otsu
_, th_otsu = cv2.threshold(blur, 0, 255, cv2.THRESH_BINARY + cv2.THRESH_OTSU)

# Adaptive
th_adapt = cv2.adaptiveThreshold(blur, 255, cv2.ADAPTIVE_THRESH_GAUSSIAN_C,
                                  cv2.THRESH_BINARY, 11, 2)

# Contours + bounding boxes
contours, _ = cv2.findContours(th_otsu, cv2.RETR_EXTERNAL, cv2.CHAIN_APPROX_SIMPLE)
annotated = cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_GRAY2BGR)
for cnt in contours:
    if cv2.contourArea(cnt) > 100:
        x, y, w, h = cv2.boundingRect(cnt)
        cv2.rectangle(annotated, (x, y), (x + w, y + h), (0, 255, 0), 2)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(8, 8))
axes[0, 0].imshow(th_global, cmap='gray'); axes[0, 0].set_title('Global T=127')
axes[0, 1].imshow(th_otsu, cmap='gray');   axes[0, 1].set_title('Otsu')
axes[1, 0].imshow(th_adapt, cmap='gray');  axes[1, 0].set_title('Adaptive')
axes[1, 1].imshow(cv2.cvtColor(annotated, cv2.COLOR_BGR2RGB)); axes[1, 1].set_title('Bounding boxes')
for ax in axes.ravel(): ax.axis('off')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
thinkAbout: Why does global thresholding fail under uneven directional lighting?
What does Otsu's method optimise, and why does it require a bimodal histogram?
How does adaptive thresholding handle smooth illumination gradients but still fail on noisy images?
applications: Automated coin, pill, and cell counting in quality assurance.
License plate localisation in automatic toll systems.
Defect region isolation in industrial inspection.
Document binarisation and text extraction in mobile scanners.
